title: Could You Report to One or More of Your Team Members
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This Field Note proposes a diagnostic question for leaders who have successfully built a high-performing team: could you, hypothetically, comfortably report to one of the people you developed? A 'yes' signals the team is mature enough that the leader should move on and replicate their team-building skill elsewhere in the organization; a 'no,' absent self-interest, signals unfinished development work remains. The piece also argues the exercise itself has value beyond diagnosis -- genuinely considering the question tends to deepen a leader's visible respect for the team, strengthening the bond regardless of the answer.
points: A diagnostic question for team maturity: could the leader comfortably report to a team member they developed?
A 'yes' answer suggests it's time for the leader to move on and build another high-performing team elsewhere.
A 'no' answer, when not self-interested, points to specific gaps still needing development work.
Simply considering the question tends to increase a leader's visible respect and admiration for their team.
Great organizations are described as unwilling to waste a leader's team-building talent by leaving them in place too long.
quotes: In the best of cases, they find themselves as the least skilled people on the team.
How comfortable would the leader be to actually report to one of the existing team members?
When a leader accepts the idea, at least in their head, that they could easily report to a team member, they inadvertently project a respect and admiration for the team that is hard to duplicate.
In cases where a leader is nowhere near accepting such a reporting line, the answer helps to create a blueprint for action about what it would take to get there.

Some questions are worth asking for the impact they have on how we see things. Asking whether you could report to one or more of your existing team members is such a question. Why not ask and learn from it?
